Series::imag¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::imag() const

What It Does¶

Returns the imaginary part of each element.

For a complex input the result is a real-valued Series of the same shape: Complex64 yields float32, Complex128 yields float64. For an input that is already real, imag() returns a zero series of the matching real dtype and shape — the imaginary part of a real number is 0.

imag() is the partner of real(); pluss::series::complex recombines the two.

Reading The Result¶

imag() extracts the second Cartesian coordinate without changing shape. A matrix remains a matrix and a scalar remains rank zero. The returned values are real numbers; the i unit is not retained in the result. If an actual complex term i * imag(z) is needed, combine a zero real component and z.imag() with pluss::series::complex.

For an already-real input, the imaginary component is identically zero. Those zeros preserve the input dtype, including integral dtypes, because no floating-point calculation is required.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series The imaginary component (all zeros for a real input). Shape is preserved; Complex64 produces float32 and Complex128 produces float64. An already-real input keeps its dtype.

Gradient¶

imag() is differentiable for a complex input: the backward lifts the real cotangent into the complex plane as a pure imaginary part (0 + grad * i), following the Wirtinger convention. For a real input the output is a constant zero, so it carries no gradient — an objective that reaches its input only through imag() of a real series is disconnected.

Examples¶

Example 1. The imaginary part of a complex series. Building the series with pluss::series::complex makes the round trip obvious — imag() returns exactly the second series that went in.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({3.0f, -1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f}),   // real parts
    pluss::make_series({4.0f,  0.0f, 2.0f, 0.0f}));  // imaginary parts

pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.imag()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[4.0000, 0.0000, 2.0000, 0.0000]

Example 2. On a real input the imaginary part is zero everywhere.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-3.0, 0.0, 2.5}).imag()
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000]

Example 3. Integral input keeps its dtype. This makes the component operation predictable in generic code even when the current batch contains no complex values.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({-3, 0, 2}).imag()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

Example 4. A matrix keeps its layout while the imaginary coordinate is extracted cell by cell.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({{3.0f, -1.0f}, {0.0f, 0.0f}}),
    pluss::make_series({{4.0f,  0.0f}, {2.0f, 0.0f}}));
pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.imag()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 4.0000 0.0000 ⎤
⎣ 2.0000 0.0000 ⎦

Example 5. The complex reverse rule lifts a real cotangent into the imaginary coordinate. Summing imag() therefore contributes 0 + 1j to every source element.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({{3.0f, -1.0f}, {0.0f, 0.0f}}),
    pluss::make_series({{4.0f,  0.0f}, {2.0f, 0.0f}}));
z.tracks_slope_(true);
z.imag().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.sensitivity()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=complex64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ (0.0000+1.0000j) (0.0000+1.0000j) ⎤
⎣ (0.0000+1.0000j) (0.0000+1.0000j) ⎦

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • On a real input imag() returns a fresh zero series, not the input — it is never a view.

  • Result dtype tracks the input precision: Complex64 -> float32.

  • For already-real input, the zero result preserves the original dtype.

  • imag() of a real leaf is a constant; do not expect a gradient through it.

Summary¶

imag() is the imaginary component of each element:

  • complex in, paired real precision out; 0 everywhere with dtype preserved for an already-real input

  • differentiable on the complex path (backward is a pure imaginary lift); no gradient on the real path

  • the counterpart of real()

See Also¶

  • Series::conj: flips the sign of this component.

  • Series::angle: the phase, atan2(imag, real).
